summary:
AGROVISION is an intelligent web platform developed for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge as a Decision Support System (DSS) to transform crop planning. By integrating international satellite data and climate models (NASA, FAO, Copernicus, USDA) with agronomic info, it evaluates 14 key variables—such as soil moisture, precipitation, temperature, and frost risk—across seven stages to rank crop compatibility for any mapped location.

The project democratizes precision agriculture and data science for farmers of varying technical backgrounds, reducing climate uncertainty without requiring physical field sensors. It helps users anticipate terrain limitations, optimize species selection, and time sowing/harvesting via customized calendars, minimizing losses and fostering sustainable practices for small-to-medium producers and researchers.

Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python, SQL, and QGIS, AGROVISION translates complex macro satellite data into transparent, justified recommendations, adapting flexibly when local soil data is missing. It features scientific rigor in variable weighting, clear distinctions between satellite estimations and direct measurements, a bilingual interface (English/Spanish), and a scalable modular architecture.

General Objective

Implement a web-based Decision Support System (DSS) focused on soil characterization and the assessment of crop agroclimatic requirements, with the aim of optimizing crop selection and sowing planning according to the environmental and agricultural conditions of each region.

Specific Objectives

  • Geographical location: Identify the user's region or allow them to select it manually.
  • Soil characterization: Analyze soil texture, pH, fertility, drainage, and other available properties.
  • Agroclimatic assessment: Consider temperature, rainfall, humidity, and seasonality.
  • Crop selection: Compare local conditions with the requirements of different crops.
  • Sowing planning: Display recommended sowing and harvesting periods using agricultural calendars.
  • Decision support: Generate recommendations and technical crop profiles to facilitate decision-making.

The main idea is that the platform should not simply display information; it should analyze the conditions of a specific region and help users determine which crops are suitable for cultivation and when it is best to sow them.

Introduction

Within the framework of the NASA International Space Apps Challenge, this project aims to transform the way farmers make strategic decisions about their crops. In the face of climate change and increasing weather variability, modern agriculture requires accurate and accessible tools that can turn complex data into practical actions.

To address this challenge, we developed a Decision Support System (DSS) based on NASA satellite and agroclimatic data. The platform integrates soil characterization, environmental variable analysis, and local agricultural calendars to optimize crop selection and sowing planning, promoting more sustainable, adaptive, and efficient agricultural production.

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 1 of 17

The primary users of the proposed Decision Support System (DSS) are farmers and agricultural producers, particularly those who need reliable information to make decisions about crop selection and sowing schedules according to the environmental conditions of their regions.

The platform is designed to support the following user groups:

  1. Farmers and Agricultural Producers: Use the system to identify suitable crops, evaluate soil and climate conditions, and plan sowing and harvesting periods.
  2. Agronomists and Agricultural Technicians: Use the platform to analyze environmental data, assess crop suitability, and provide technical recommendations to producers.
  3. Agricultural Students and Researchers: Access soil, climate, and crop information for educational, scientific, and research purposes.
  4. Agricultural Advisors and Organizations: Use the system to support regional agricultural planning and promote more sustainable production practices.

Primary Target Audience: Farmers and small- to medium-scale agricultural producers who need accessible, data-driven tools to improve crop selection and agricultural planning.

System Purpose: To make satellite and agroclimatic information accessible and understandable, helping users with different levels of technical knowledge make more informed agricultural decisions.

1. Development: AGROVISION – Agricultural Guidance Platform

Modern agriculture increasingly requires information to make decisions regarding crop selection, planting dates, water management, and the assessment of soil conditions. Factors such as temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, solar radiation, altitude, and soil characteristics directly influence plant growth and development.

In this context, precision agriculture uses digital technologies, geographic information systems, meteorological data, satellite imagery, and analytical tools to study the conditions of a specific region and improve agricultural planning.

AGROVISION is a web-based agricultural guidance platform designed to gather information from different scientific sources and international organizations. Its purpose is to analyze the environmental and geographical characteristics of a location in order to identify which crops could grow there and what their main limitations might be.

The system aims to transform large amounts of environmental data into understandable and useful information for farmers and agricultural producers. To achieve this, it combines satellite, historical, meteorological, and agronomic data with an analytical engine that compares the conditions of a given area with the requirements of different crops.

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 2 of 17

1.1. Precision Agriculture

Precision agriculture is a production approach that uses information technologies to analyze land variability and make agricultural decisions based on the specific conditions of each location. The technologies used include Global Positioning Systems (GPS), Geographic Information Systems (GIS), weather sensors, satellite imagery, agricultural databases, and mathematical and statistical models.

AGROVISION incorporates these concepts through the analysis of geographical, climatic, and agricultural variables, making it possible to assess the compatibility between the conditions of a region and the requirements of each crop.

1.2. Remote Sensing and Satellite Observation

Remote sensing involves obtaining information about the Earth's surface through sensors installed on satellites or other platforms, without the need to perform direct measurements at every point on the ground.

These sensors record different surface characteristics, such as moisture, temperature, radiation, and changes in land cover. This data can be used to study the environmental conditions of a region and monitor how they evolve over time.

AGROVISION considers the use of NASA satellite products to incorporate information related to soil moisture, precipitation, land surface temperature, and topography.

It is important to distinguish satellite data from measurements taken directly in the field. Satellite products represent estimates or indirect measurements and may have limitations regarding spatial resolution, coverage, and update frequency.

1.3. Meteorological and Climate Information

Weather conditions directly influence crop development. Temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, solar radiation, and wind are fundamental variables for assessing the environment in which a plant will grow.

Meteorological information describes atmospheric conditions at a specific moment or during a particular period, whereas climate information makes it possible to study the behavior of these variables over extended periods.

For AGROVISION, this data makes it possible to identify periods of high or low temperatures, analyze the annual distribution of precipitation, study the frequency of dry periods, assess frost risk, and compare different years and seasons.

1.4. Soil Characteristics

Soil is the medium in which roots develop and from which plants obtain water and nutrients. Its physical and chemical characteristics influence resource availability and agricultural productivity.

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 3 of 17

The most important variables include:

  • Soil moisture: represents the amount of water present in the soil.
  • pH: indicates the degree of acidity or alkalinity and affects nutrient availability.
  • Organic matter: contributes to soil structure, fertility, and water retention.
  • Texture: depends on the proportions of sand, silt, and clay.
  • Drainage: determines the soil's ability to remove excess water.

AGROVISION considers these parameters as part of its agricultural suitability analysis. However, not all of them can be accurately obtained through satellite information. When reliable data is unavailable, the system must allow users to enter the information manually or indicate that it is not available.

1.5. Geographic Information Systems (GIS)

Geographic Information Systems make it possible to store, process, analyze, and represent data associated with geographical locations.

Using latitude and longitude coordinates, it is possible to link a location to different layers of information, such as precipitation, temperature, elevation, land cover, and environmental characteristics.

In AGROVISION, GIS technologies make it possible to connect the location selected by the user with data from external sources and present the results through maps and visualizations.

1.6. Statistical Analysis Applied to Climate

Statistical analysis makes it possible to study the behavior of environmental variables over time. Historical records can be used to calculate averages, maximum and minimum values, standard deviations, variability, and the frequency of extreme events.

One of the tools that can be used is the normal distribution, also known as the Gaussian distribution or bell curve. It represents how certain values are distributed around a mean, provided that the data is compatible with this statistical model.

AGROVISION considers using distribution curves to study temperatures and compare different periods or years. However, the normal distribution should not be applied automatically: its suitability for the analyzed data must first be verified. Otherwise, histograms, box plots, percentiles, or alternative distributions can be used.

1.7. Artificial Intelligence and Recommendation Systems

Recommendation systems use available information to compare alternatives and generate suggestions based on specific criteria. In agriculture, they can compare the requirements of a crop with the climatic, geographical, and soil conditions of a region.

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 4 of 17

AGROVISION proposes a recommendation engine that analyzes available variables and generates a ranking of compatible crops. Each result must include an explanation of favorable factors, identified limitations, and unavailable information.

Artificial intelligence can assist in software development, information organization, and result interpretation. However, agronomic recommendations must be based on verifiable data and technical criteria, not solely on responses generated by a language model.

2. General Operation of AGROVISION

The platform operates through a series of stages that transform a geographical location into an agricultural analysis:

  1. Location selection: The user enters a place name, selects a point on the map, or provides geographical coordinates.
  2. Data acquisition: The application queries the available information sources for that location.
  3. Processing: The data is organized, validated, and converted into variables that can be used by the system.
  4. Environmental analysis: Climatic, geographical, and soil conditions are examined.
  5. Agronomic comparison: The area's conditions are compared with the requirements of each crop.
  6. Recommendation generation: The engine calculates compatibility and ranks crops according to the results.
  7. Visualization: The user views the results through the dashboard, maps, charts, and crop profiles.

3. Information Sources Used by AGROVISION

To ensure that its recommendations are scientifically grounded, AGROVISION is designed to integrate different information sources. Each one fulfills a specific function within the analysis.

Including a source in the project design does not mean that it is already connected to the code. Its integration must be implemented and verified during development.

3.1. NASA Sources

3.1.1. NASA SMAP – Soil Moisture

SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive) is a NASA satellite mission designed to study soil moisture. Its products provide estimates of surface soil moisture and, through modeled products, information about root-zone soil moisture.

In AGROVISION, this data can be used to analyze water availability, identify drought periods, and assess the water conditions of a location.

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 5 of 17

The information must be interpreted according to the spatial resolution of the selected product and the difference between surface moisture and root-zone moisture. It does not replace direct soil measurements.

Official source: https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/platforms/space-based-platforms/smap

3.1.2. NASA GPM – Precipitation

The GPM (Global Precipitation Measurement) project combines information from different satellites to estimate precipitation across various regions of the planet.

One of its main products is IMERG, which provides precipitation estimates at an approximate spatial resolution of 0.1° and records every 30 minutes. Different processing versions are available, with varying delivery times and processing levels.

AGROVISION can use this information to calculate daily, monthly, and annual precipitation totals, identify dry periods, and analyze rainfall distribution.

Official source: https://gpm.nasa.gov/data

3.1.3. NASA ECOSTRESS – Land Surface Temperature and Evapotranspiration

ECOSTRESS is an Earth-observation instrument installed on the International Space Station. Its products make it possible to study land surface temperature and evapotranspiration.

The mission aims to understand how plants respond to heat and water stress and how they use water.

In AGROVISION, this information can complement the analysis of vegetation thermal conditions. However, land surface temperature must not be confused with air temperature, which is commonly used to assess meteorological frost risk.

Official source: https://ecostress.jpl.nasa.gov/data

3.1.4. NASA SRTM – Terrain Elevation

SRTM (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission) is a mission that provided topographic information for a large portion of the Earth's surface using radar technology.

Its digital elevation models make it possible to estimate the altitude of a location and, through terrain analysis, obtain slope information.

In AGROVISION, this data can help study terrain characteristics and complement agricultural suitability assessments.

Official source: https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/instruments/srtm

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 6 of 17

3.2. Agricultural and Climate Organization Sources

3.2.1. FAO GAEZ – Agro-Ecological Suitability

GAEZ (Global Agro-Ecological Zones) is a methodology and database developed by the FAO and IIASA to assess agro-ecological resources and land suitability for different crops.

It includes information on soil and water resources, agro-climatic conditions, crop suitability, and potential productivity.

AGROVISION can use this information as a reference to compare crop requirements with the environmental conditions of a region.

Official source: https://gaez.fao.org/

3.2.2. Copernicus ERA5 – Historical Meteorological Information

ERA5 is a climate reanalysis dataset that combines meteorological observations with numerical models to reconstruct atmospheric conditions over time.

It provides variables such as air temperature, precipitation, humidity, solar radiation, and wind. Its hourly surface-level data has an approximate grid resolution of 0.25° and can be downloaded through the Climate Data Store in formats such as NetCDF and CSV.

In AGROVISION, ERA5 can be used to study historical climate patterns, calculate mean, maximum, and minimum temperatures, analyze frost periods, and compare different years.

It must be identified as reanalysis data, rather than direct measurements taken on the ground or a weather forecast.

Official source: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/

3.2.3. USDA Ag Data Commons – Agricultural Databases

Ag Data Commons is a repository of datasets related to agriculture and agricultural research. It can be used to locate information about crops, production, soils, and agronomic characteristics.

For AGROVISION, each dataset must be evaluated before being incorporated, checking its geographical coverage, date, methodology, and usefulness.

Official source: https://www.nal.usda.gov/services/agdatacommons

3.2.4. USDA CropScape – Geographical Distribution of Crops

CropScape provides access to geographical information about crop distribution, primarily through the United States Cropland Data Layer.

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 7 of 17

It can be useful as a methodological reference or for areas covered by its data. However, it must not be used as a source of previous crop information for locations in Argentina without verifying that valid coverage exists.

Official source: https://nassgeodata.gmu.edu/CropScape/

Integration must be carried out through documented services, catalogs, APIs, or official downloads. Depending on the product, an account, access credentials, or geospatial processing tools may be required.

Formats may include JSON, CSV, NetCDF, HDF5, and GeoTIFF. Each format requires specific reading, processing, and conversion procedures before its data can be used within the application.

4. Main AGROVISION Features

4.1. Geographical Selection

Users will be able to enter a location or select a point using a map. Based on its coordinates, the system will search for the corresponding environmental data. The selected location will serve as the starting point for all subsequent analyses.

4.2. Agricultural Dashboard

The dashboard will provide a centralized visualization of the most important variables:

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 8 of 17

  • Temperature and atmospheric humidity.
  • Precipitation.
  • Soil moisture.
  • Solar radiation.
  • Daylight hours.
  • Frost risk.
  • Altitude and slope.
  • Agricultural suitability indicators.

Information will be organized into cards, charts, and sections to facilitate interpretation.

4.3. Crop Profiles

Each crop may have a profile containing its main characteristics:

  • Common name and scientific name.
  • Botanical family.
  • Temperature requirements.
  • Water requirements.
  • Soil and pH requirements.
  • Light and photoperiod requirements.
  • Planting season.
  • Harvest season.
  • Approximate growing cycle duration.
  • Frost sensitivity.
  • Suitability for the selected location.

These profiles will make it possible to compare the requirements of each species with the conditions of the region.

4.4. Agricultural Calendar

The calendar will display planting, growing, and harvesting periods for different crops. Its information must be adapted to the selected geographical location, since dates may vary depending on the region, climate, and cultivated variety.

4.5. Climate Charts

The application will allow users to study environmental variables through statistical charts. For temperatures, it will be possible to represent mean, maximum, and minimum temperatures, record distributions, temperature variability, extreme values, and comparisons between years.

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 9 of 17

The Gaussian bell curve may be used when justified by the distribution of the data. If records do not follow a normal distribution, other statistical charts that accurately represent their behavior will be used.

4.6. Language System

AGROVISION includes a language selector to switch between English and Spanish, with English as the default language. The system must translate menus, buttons, headings, messages, crop profiles, and recommendations while preserving scientific names and technical units.

4.7. Land Characteristics Form

The form will allow users to enter additional information about their land. Certain parameters will be optional:

  • Organic matter percentage.
  • Soil moisture.
  • pH.
  • Previous crops.

This will allow users to obtain an initial analysis even if they do not know all the characteristics of their land. When data is missing, the application must report this limitation and continue using the available variables without inventing measurements.

5. Agricultural Recommendation System

The recommendation engine is one of the central components of AGROVISION. Its purpose is to compare the conditions of a location with the agronomic requirements of different crops to determine which ones have the highest compatibility.

5.1. Variables Considered

The system may analyze:

  1. Mean, maximum, and minimum temperatures.
  2. Accumulated precipitation.
  3. Soil moisture.
  4. Atmospheric humidity.
  5. Daylight hours and photoperiod.
  6. Frost risk.
  7. Freeze-thaw cycles.
  8. Altitude and slope.
  9. Soil pH.
  10. Organic matter.

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 10 of 17

  1. Previous crops.
  2. Agro-ecological suitability.
  3. Heat and water stress.
  4. Seasonality and growing cycle duration.

5.2. Requirements Comparison

Each crop has environmental conditions that are necessary for proper development. For example, a crop may require moderate temperatures, a certain level of water availability, and a sufficiently long frost-free period. The system will compare these requirements with the data available for the selected location.

5.3. Results Classification

Recommendations may be classified into four categories:

Category

Interpretation

Favorable

Available conditions largely match the crop's requirements

Moderately Favorable

Some limitations exist but could potentially be managed

Limiting

One or more factors may hinder development

Unfavorable

Conditions present significant incompatibilities

5.4. Scoring System

To rank crops, a scoring system based on the compatibility between each species' requirements and the conditions of the selected location is proposed. The weights assigned to the variables must be justified through agronomic literature, scientific studies, and documented crop requirements.

Not all variables will necessarily have the same importance. For example, frost risk may be decisive for a sensitive species, while having a smaller influence on another.

When information is missing, the system must calculate the score using only the available variables and display the level of information used. The absence of data must not be interpreted as a favorable or unfavorable condition.

5.5. Explanation of Recommendations

Each recommended crop must provide an understandable explanation including:

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 11 of 17

  • Why it was selected.
  • Which conditions favor its development.
  • Which limitations were identified.
  • Which information is unavailable.
  • Which factors should be verified before making a production decision.

This will allow AGROVISION to become more than just an application that displays results. It will also be a tool that explains how those results were obtained.

6. Incorporation of New Agricultural Variables

In addition to meteorological and soil variables, AGROVISION aims to incorporate indicators that make it possible to study important aspects of crop development.

6.1. Daylight Hours and Photoperiod

Photoperiod is the duration of the daily light period. It influences several physiological processes in plants, such as flowering, growth, and development. AGROVISION will be able to calculate approximate daylight hours using geographical latitude and date. These values will make it possible to study seasonal variations and relate them to the requirements of each species.

6.2. Freeze-Thaw Cycles

Freeze-thaw cycles can influence the physical properties of soil and the growing conditions of crops. Historical air temperature records and, when available, soil temperature data can be used to analyze these cycles. The system may identify consecutive periods with temperatures below zero followed by periods with temperatures above that threshold. This will make it possible to estimate the frequency of these events.

6.3. Frost Risk

Frost is an important factor in agricultural planning, particularly for crops that are sensitive to low temperatures. AGROVISION may use historical minimum temperatures and available meteorological data to identify periods with greater risk.

The assessment must consider minimum temperatures, the historical frequency of below-zero temperatures, the times of the year with the highest risk, crop sensitivity, and the plant's development stage.

It is important to clarify that an air temperature below 0°C does not necessarily mean that all crops will suffer the same damage. Sensitivity depends on the species, variety, and stage of development.

7. Benefits of AGROVISION

The implementation of this platform may provide several benefits to the agricultural sector:

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 12 of 17

  1. Improved crop planning: Makes it possible to compare regional conditions with the requirements of different species before starting production.
  2. Access to scientific information: Brings together data from international organizations and projects, reducing dependence on isolated sources of information.
  3. Climate condition analysis: Facilitates the study of temperatures, precipitation, humidity, and meteorological risks.
  4. Use of geographical information: Makes it possible to relate land characteristics to their location and environmental conditions.
  5. Identification of limitations: Helps recognize factors that could hinder crop development.
  6. Agricultural information management: Integrates crop profiles, calendars, and environmental variables into a single platform.
  7. Accessibility: Aims to present technical information clearly so that it can be understood by people who do not necessarily have advanced knowledge of meteorology or data analysis.
  8. Support for production decisions: Provides information that can complement the producer's experience and consultations with agricultural professionals.

8. Objectives and Expected Results

The ultimate objective is to develop an intelligent agricultural web platform capable of integrating information from different sources and transforming it into understandable recommendations.

AGROVISION is expected to allow users to:

  • Consult the environmental conditions of a location.
  • Identify crops compatible with a region.
  • Analyze meteorological and historical information.
  • Recognize potential agricultural limitations.
  • Consult planting and harvesting calendars.
  • Visualize data through maps and charts.
  • Compare the requirements of different crops.
  • Obtain explained and scientifically grounded recommendations.

In the long term, the aim is to expand the number of available crops, improve analytical accuracy, and incorporate new agricultural information sources.

The platform is not intended to replace professional agronomic advice or guarantee production results. Its purpose is to provide technical information that helps evaluate alternatives and make better-informed decisions.

9.1. Hardware Resources

The project mainly requires:

  • A computer for programming and testing the application.
  • An internet connection to access services and repositories.
  • Sufficient RAM and processing capacity to work with the development environment.
  • A server or hosting service to publish the platform when necessary.

There is no need to build satellites or own sensors to access the public datasets mentioned. The information is obtained through the platforms and services provided by those organizations.

10. Use of Artificial Intelligence During Development

Artificial intelligence tools can be used to support different stages of AGROVISION's development. Their potential applications include:

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data — AGROVISIONPage 14 of 17

  • Understanding existing code structures.
  • Identifying programming errors.
  • Suggesting improvements to software organization.
  • Assisting with API integration.
  • Explaining technical documentation.
  • Organizing variables and datasets.
  • Supporting interface design.
  • Preparing documentation and explanations of how the system works.

Artificial intelligence can also help interpret results and organize recommendations. However, this assistance must be distinguished from actual data processing. Meteorological values, crop characteristics, and statistical results must come from verifiable sources or reproducible calculations. AI must not invent information when data is missing.

13. Conclusion

AGROVISION proposes integrating programming tools, satellite information, agricultural databases, meteorological analysis, and geographic information systems to develop an agricultural guidance platform.

Its main contribution lies in bringing together different environmental and agronomic variables to assess the compatibility between the conditions of a location and the requirements of different crops.

The use of sources such as NASA, FAO, USDA, and Copernicus makes it possible to incorporate scientific information that can contribute to improving the assessment of agricultural conditions.

Through data processing, the platform aims to generate understandable recommendations, identify potential limitations, and facilitate the planning of production activities.

The development of AGROVISION represents an application of technology to the agricultural sector, demonstrating how computer science, data science, and Earth observation can work together to provide useful information for decision-making.
